Gardner CNRA:
Gardner visually operates as four distinct districts contained within the overall project area boundaries.
Gardner appears to have been one of San Jose's earlier street-car or automobile suburbs. The primary development of the area probably occurred during 1910-1935. Thus, the housing consists mostly of Victorian-derivative and bungalow styles. The original main streets likely were Bird Avenue and Delmas Avenue, which run north-south between the downtown and still fashionable further removed (e.g. Willow Glen).
The street pattern of Gardner creates some visual interest. Basically still a grid, the later developed areas show a greater variety in layout that did Olinder or Northside. The Northern section of Gardner (north of the railroad embankment) has its long axis of the grid running north-south; south of the railroad the main axis is east-west; and in the extreme southwestern corner of the project area the grid turns 45 degrees to connect to the northwest-southeast pattern of the neighborhoods across Willow Street.
The different orientations of the grid pattern help reinforce the feeling of separate districts within the overall Gardner area. The project boundaries and also man-made barriers which traverse the area serve to define these districts.
One sub-area is bounded by Highway 280 on the west and north, the Palm Haven Subdivision to the south, and the recently-widened Bird Avenue to the east. Bird Avenue, expanded to an expressway scale, separates this small district from the remainder of Gardner; Highway 280 creates a strong image of isolation. The dwellings within this sub-area appear slightly older generally (and perhaps more deteriorated) than those across Bird Avenue. (The exception would be the newer homes fronting on Harrison Street.) This district for the most part lacks a coherent street landscape. However, the pact of strong isolation suggests possibilities of community which in turn give this sub-area a high potential for improvement. The vestigial commercial uses along Bird Avenue and the industrial functions and irregular vacant parcels seem to strengthen the self-contained quality of this district.
East of Bird Avenue and north of the railroad tracks is a second district. This sub-area too is isolated; in fact, all of Gardner has been so isolated by freeways that potential deterioration passed it by and thus its original integrity has been largely preserved. In this second district, the usually thick presence of street landscaping seems to bring out the area's charm, even visually overcoming the destructive effects of widespread land subsidence. In fact, where recent street improvements have been constructed, no provision for landscaping was made, and some of charm is thus jeopardized. This district overall possesses an intimate, human scale, which is further enhanced by the presence of open space and parks and the railroad embankment, which by its being elevated above-grade, visually closes and tightens the neighborhood.
